ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The horizontal axis of the spectrum is Mass Number (amu), from about 122 to 130; the vertical axis is Relative Abundance (%). There are multiple peaks near 122, 123, 124, 125, 126, 128, and 130 amu in the graph, among which the peaks at 128 and 130 amu are relatively high; there is no peak at 127 amu. Reasoning: A mass spectrometer separates samples according to isotope mass, so every naturally occurring isotope in the sample should have a peak at its mass number. Natural iodine has only one isotope, I-127; the atomic number of iodine is 53, so I-127 has 127 - 53 = 74 neutrons. If the sample contains iodine, a peak at 127 amu should appear. The spectrum has no 127 amu peak, so it does not support containing iodine. On the other hand, the spectrum shows peaks at multiple mass numbers, which is consistent with tellurium having multiple naturally occurring isotopes. Therefore, the key fact supporting the sample being pure Te is: iodine has only one naturally occurring isotope, I-127 (74 neutrons), while tellurium has multiple naturally occurring isotopes.

method.method_draft: First describe the spectrum: it contains several isotope-mass peaks for masses near 122–130 amu but lacks a peak at 127 amu. From the text, the sample was thought to contain I and Te and the mass spectrometer separates isotopes by mass. Apply the rule that each naturally occurring isotope of an element would appear at its isotope mass. Since naturally occurring iodine is only I-127, a mixture containing iodine should show a 127-amu peak. The absence of that peak supports that there is no iodine, while the multiple peaks are consistent with tellurium’s multiple natural isotopes. Conclude the needed fact is that iodine has only one naturally occurring isotope, I-127 with 74 neutrons, whereas tellurium has more than one naturally occurring isotope.
